bank.topic: Theranos: a $9 billion valuation, a 2015 Wall Street Journal exposé and an 11-year sentence for Elizabeth Holmes (2022)
bank.hook: At its peak, private investors valued Theranos at about $9 billion. Its founder later got 135 months in prison.
bank.body: Thread on Theranos and the one question that would have saved investors billions.
parts:
At its peak, private investors valued a blood-testing startup at about $9 billion.

Its founder was later sentenced to 135 months in prison.

The gap between those numbers is one unasked question.

Elizabeth Holmes founded Theranos in 2003, after leaving Stanford at 19.

The pitch: run a wide range of lab tests from a few drops of blood from a finger prick.

It sounded like the future.

Board seats, partnerships, glowing magazine covers.

The valuation climbed to about $9 billion, and Holmes became a paper billionaire.

What almost nobody had was independent proof the machines worked.

In 2015, The Wall Street Journal reported that the technology was struggling to do what the company claimed.

The story came from reporting and insiders who were willing to talk.

2018: Theranos shuts down.

January 2022: a jury convicts Holmes on four counts of fraud.

November 18, 2022: Judge Edward Davila sentences her to 11 years and 3 months.

The question that would have saved billions: "Show me it working, checked by someone who isn't paid by you."

Use it this week on any big claim: a product, a deal, a pitch, an AI tool.
bank.cta: What's a claim you've accepted at work without independent proof?
bank.moneyAngle: High-engagement fraud story thread; builds authority on decision-making and due diligence.

bank.topic: Roger Boisjoly's 1985 O-ring memo and the 'take off your engineering hat' moment before Challenger (1986)
bank.hook: Six months before Challenger, an engineer put his warning in writing: "The result would be a catastrophe of the highest order."
bank.body:
Roger Boisjoly worked on the shuttle's solid rocket boosters at Morton Thiokol. His memo, dated 31 July 1985, warned that the O-ring seals in the booster joints could fail.

On the night of 27 January 1986, with record cold forecast, he and other Thiokol engineers argued against launching. Cold would make the O-rings worse at sealing.

In a break in the call, senior manager Jerald Mason told engineering VP Bob Lund to "take off your engineering hat and put on your management hat." Lund changed his vote.

The next morning it was 36°F at launch, colder than any previous shuttle launch. Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff.

The lesson isn't "be braver". It's design. If your team's dissent can be outvoted by changing hats, your process is the risk.

This week, ask your team one question before a big decision: "What would make this fail, and who here thinks it might?" Then give that person the floor first.
bank.cta: How does your team make it safe to say "don't launch"?
bank.moneyAngle: Serious leadership story that earns saves and comments from managers; supports decision-making content.

bank.topic: The strength of weak ties: most jobs found through contacts came via people seen only occasionally or rarely (Granovetter, 1973)
bank.hook: In the 1970s a sociologist asked 282 men how they found their jobs. The answer wasn't their best friends.
bank.body:
Mark Granovetter studied men in the Boston area who had found work through a personal contact.

Only 16.7% said they saw that contact often.
55.6% saw them occasionally.
27.8% saw them rarely, once a year or less.

He called it "the strength of weak ties" (1973). Your close friends know what you know. Acquaintances know about the jobs, people and chances you haven't heard of.

In 2022, researchers from LinkedIn, MIT, Stanford and Harvard tested it on about 20 million users over five years. Moderately weak ties helped job moves the most.

Your move today: message one person you haven't spoken to in a year. No ask. Just "saw this and thought of you."
bank.cta: Who's the one person you'd message first?
bank.moneyAngle: Relatable relationship-and-career science that drives comments and shares.

bank.topic: Benjamin Franklin's 200-year bequest: £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia (1790–1990)
bank.hook: Benjamin Franklin left £1,000 each to two cities, with a 200-year timer.
bank.body:
Benjamin Franklin left £1,000 each to two cities, with a 200-year timer.

He projected each would grow to more than £4 million. In 1990 Boston's fund was almost $5 million and Philadelphia's about $2 million. Compounding worked; the plan around it didn't keep up. Swipe for the story.

When did you last review your own long-term plan?
parts: Benjamin Franklin left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia, with a 200-year timer.
He died in 1790. The money was to be lent to young married tradesmen at 5% interest.
His projection: £131,000 per city after 100 years.
And £4,061,000 per city after 200 years.
Philadelphia, 1907: the fund held $172,350, less than a fourth of his projection.
1990: Boston's fund was almost $5 million. Philadelphia's was about $2 million.
Why so short? The apprentice system his loans depended on faded away.
Compounding worked. The plan around it didn't keep up with the world.
Your move: automate it, review it once a year, and update the plan when life changes.
bank.cta: Save this and put a yearly money review in your calendar.

factCheck: The Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre on Monday, August 21, 1911 (History Today, History.com).
The thief, Vincenzo Peruggia, had worked at the Louvre as a handyman and helped build the painting's protective frame (History.com).
He hid in a storage closet on the evening of Sunday, August 20, and took the painting around 7:15 the next morning while the museum was closed (History.com).
He wore a white apron like museum employees and left the glass frame in a service stairwell (History.com).
Finding the courtyard door locked, he tried to take the doorknob apart; a plumber helped him open it (History.com).
Staff didn't notice the theft until around noon on Tuesday (History.com).
Police searched cars, ship passengers and pedestrians; when the Louvre reopened about a week later, thousands came to see the empty wall (History.com).
Guillaume Apollinaire was arrested in September 1911; Pablo Picasso was also a suspect; both were cleared (History Today, History.com).
Peruggia kept the painting about two years in a trunk with a false bottom (History.com, History Today).
In December 1913 he offered it to Florence dealer Alfredo Geri for 500,000 lire; Geri consulted Uffizi director Giovanni Poggi; Peruggia was arrested at his hotel on December 11, 1913 (History.com).
He was sentenced to one year and 15 days and served about seven months (History.com).
The theft is widely credited with making the Mona Lisa world-famous (History.com).

items.topic: Cursor's AI support bot 'Sam' invented a login policy and users cancelled (April 2025)
items.hook: April 2025: an AI support bot made up a company rule. Customers started cancelling.
items.body: Thread on the Cursor support-bot incident and how to stop your own AI from inventing policy.
parts:
April 2025. Developers using Cursor, a popular AI coding tool, kept getting logged out every time they switched computers.

They emailed support. Support answered fast.

Too fast.

The reply came from 'Sam'. Sam explained this was expected: one subscription couldn't stay logged in on several devices.

Clear. Confident. Official-sounding.

One problem.

There was no such policy.

Sam was an AI support bot, and it had invented the rule.

By the time anyone noticed, the complaint was spreading on Reddit and users were posting that they'd cancel.

Co-founder Michael Truell replied on Reddit: "We have no such policy."

The logouts came from a recent session-security change. The user who raised it got a refund.

Then the real fix: Truell said AI-generated replies to support emails would now be clearly labeled.

An AI company, burned by its own AI's confidence.

The pattern to remember: a model that doesn't know will often still answer, in the same calm tone it uses when it's right.

Confidence is not a source.

Today: ask your AI assistant about one rule at your company you already know cold.

If it invents a policy, it will invent one for your customers too. Give it the real docs and route anything about rules or money to a human.
items.cta: Run the one-question test on your AI tool today.

items.topic: The Mechanical Turk: the 1770 'chess machine' with a human inside
items.hook:
In 1809, Napoleon played chess against a machine and lost.

The machine had a person inside it.
items.body:
The Turk was built in 1770 by Wolfgang von Kempelen to impress Empress Maria Theresa: a carved figure seated at a cabinet full of gears, beating visitors at chess.

It toured Europe and America for decades. Benjamin Franklin lost to it. Charles Babbage lost to it.

The secret: a strong human player hid inside the cabinet, tracking the board through magnets under each square.

In 1836 Edgar Allan Poe published an essay arguing it had to be a hoax. The Turk burned in a Philadelphia museum fire on July 5, 1854.

In 2005 Amazon named its crowd-work marketplace after it: Mechanical Turk.

Why this matters now: plenty of products sold as "AI" still run on people, rules or luck behind the curtain. That isn't always bad. Not knowing is.

Before you buy or build on an AI tool, ask three things:
1. What does the model do, and what do humans do?
2. What happens when it's unsure?
3. Can I see it fail on my own data?

items.topic: Enron: $90.75 to $0.26, and the 401(k) plan that was 62% Enron stock (2000–2001)
items.hook: $90.75 to $0.26 in 15 months. Many of the people hit hardest worked there.
items.body:
In August 2000, Enron stock hit $90.75. On November 30, 2001, it closed at $0.26.

At the end of 2000, 62% of the assets in Enron's employee 401(k) plan were Enron stock. When the company failed, many people lost their job and a large part of their retirement savings in the same few weeks.

You don't have to predict fraud to protect yourself. You just have to stop one company from being your salary, your bonus and your savings all at once.

Swipe for the timeline. How much of your net worth depends on your employer today?
parts: $90.75 to $0.26 in 15 months. Many of the people hit hardest worked there.
August 2000: Enron stock hits $90.75. It's one of America's most admired companies.
Fortune's survey names it America's most innovative large company.
Inside the employee 401(k) plan, 62% of assets are Enron stock (end of 2000).
Aug 14, 2001: CEO Jeff Skilling resigns. The next day, Sherron Watkins sends an anonymous warning letter.
Oct 16, 2001: restatements cut shareholders' equity by $1.2 billion.
Nov 30, 2001: the stock closes at $0.26. Two days later, Enron files for Chapter 11 with $63.4 billion in assets.
Employees lose jobs and retirement savings at the same time. Pension losses: about $2 billion.
The lesson: never let one company be your paycheck, your bonus and your savings.

items.topic: The pratfall effect: the quiz star who spilled coffee (Aronson, 1966)
items.hook: In 1966, a psychologist made a near-perfect student spill coffee all over his new suit. On purpose.
items.body:
Elliot Aronson and his colleagues played University of Minnesota students a tape of a young man trying out for a College Quiz Bowl team.

In one version he was brilliant: 92% of the hard questions right, honor student, yearbook editor, track team.

In another, he was average: 30% right.

Then, near the end of some tapes, you hear a clatter, and the contestant groans that he's spilled coffee all over his new suit.

The result: the brilliant contestant who spilled coffee was rated the most likable of all. The same accident made the average contestant less likable.

Researchers call it the pratfall effect. Once people see you're capable, a small, human mistake can make you easier to like. It only works on top of competence, not instead of it.

So stop hiding every tiny mess-up from the people you care about. Laugh at the spilled coffee.

items.topic: FDR's 300/190 blood pressure and the birth of the Framingham Heart Study (1945–1948)
items.hook: The President's blood pressure was 300/190. His doctor called the rise normal for his age.
items.body:
The President's blood pressure was 300/190. His doctor called the rise normal for his age.

Franklin D. Roosevelt died of a cerebral hemorrhage on April 12, 1945. Three years later, the National Heart Act funded a study in one small town that changed how we think about heart health.

Swipe for the story, then go check your own numbers. When did you last have your blood pressure taken?
parts: The President's blood pressure was 300/190.
Back then, rising blood pressure was seen as part of normal aging. No treatment was considered.
A common rule of thumb: an acceptable systolic was about 100 plus your age.
April 12, 1945: Roosevelt dies of a cerebral hemorrhage at 63. His pressure at death: 300/190.
1948: President Truman signs the National Heart Act.
October 1948: the Framingham Heart Study begins in Massachusetts. 5,209 residents aged 28 to 62 sign up.
1961: Framingham researchers publish on 'risk factors' for heart disease. High blood pressure is one of the big ones.
The habit that came out of it: know your numbers. Get checked, and ask a professional what yours mean.
items.cta: Save this and book a blood pressure check this month.

factCheck: On May 6, 2010, the Dow briefly fell more than 1,000 points, temporarily wiping out nearly $1 trillion in market value (AP/Yahoo Finance, Jan 2020).
Most of the drop reversed within minutes the same afternoon.
Navinder Sarao was a London-based futures trader; his company was registered at a small house in Hounslow, west London (Fortune, Apr 2015).
He traded S&P 500 E-mini futures; prosecutors said he used 'spoofing': large orders he intended to cancel.
US authorities said his trading contributed to the flash crash.
He was arrested in London in April 2015 and pleaded guilty in 2016 to wire fraud and spoofing.
The DOJ complaint said he made $879,018 on May 6, 2010 (Fortune).
Fortune reported he allegedly made more than $4 million on August 4, 2011.
In January 2020, Judge Virginia Kendall sentenced him to time served plus one year of home confinement (not in the script).

bank.topic: Google's AI Overviews told users to put glue on pizza, sourced from an 11-year-old Reddit joke (May 2024)
bank.hook: May 2024: Google's AI told people to add glue to their pizza sauce.
bank.body: Thread on the glue-pizza answer and how to check where an AI answer came from.
parts:
May 2024. Someone asks Google why cheese slides off their pizza.

Google's new AI Overview, sitting above every link, answers with confidence:

Add about 1/8 cup of non-toxic glue to the sauce.

It wasn't a hack or a fake screenshot. People traced the advice to its source within days.

A Reddit comment. Posted 11 years earlier. Written as a joke.

The same week, AI Overviews told people to eat at least one small rock a day, attributing it to UC Berkeley geologists.

That one came from a satirical article.

Google said most AI Overviews were high quality and that many viral examples were uncommon queries, doctored or impossible to reproduce. It said it was taking action on the bad ones.

But the screenshots had already gone everywhere.

The mechanism matters more than the meme: the model summarized what it found. It had no sense that a joke is a joke.

A fluent summary of a bad source is still a bad source.

Today: for any AI answer you'll act on, click through to the source it used.

If you can't find one, or it's a forum joke, treat the answer like a rumor.
bank.cta: Click through to the source on your next AI answer.
bank.moneyAngle: Funny, true AI story with high repost potential; feeds AI literacy content.

bank.topic: Abraham Wald and the planes that didn't come back (Statistical Research Group, 1943)
bank.hook:
In WWII, a mathematician was handed data on the planes that came back.

His key insight was about the ones that didn't.
bank.body:
Abraham Wald was one of the first members of the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, set up in 1942 to solve military problems with math.

Around 1943 he wrote a series of memos on aircraft survivability: how to estimate a plane's chance of surviving hits using only damage data from the planes that returned.

The logic is now famous. If you only study survivors, the hits you never see are the ones that brought planes down. Damage in the data marks where a plane can take a hit and still fly home.

The popular retelling, with the dramatic meeting and the bullet-hole diagram, is mostly a later reconstruction. The memos themselves are math, not speeches. The principle still holds.

At work, survivorship bias shows up everywhere: studying only the startups that made it, only the customers who stayed, only the projects that shipped.

The question to ask in your next review: who isn't in this data, and why?
bank.cta: Ask 'who isn't in this data?' in your next meeting.
bank.moneyAngle: Mental-model post for managers; strong saves and comments from analytical professionals.

bank.topic: The spotlight effect: the Barry Manilow T-shirt study (Cornell, 2000)
bank.hook: Cornell researchers made students walk into a room wearing a Barry Manilow T-shirt. Then they asked who noticed.
bank.body:
The shirt was chosen because it was embarrassing. Other students had rated it 9.5 on a 13-point embarrassment scale.

Each volunteer put it on and walked into a room of peers filling out questionnaires. Afterwards, the wearer guessed how many people had noticed the shirt.

Their guess: about 46%.

The real number: about 23%.

Thomas Gilovich and his colleagues called it the spotlight effect. We feel like we're on stage. Everyone else is busy starring in their own show.

This matters for relationships more than shirts. The thing you're sure your date noticed, the awkward line you replayed all night, the moment you think your friends are still talking about: most people saw half as much as you think, and forgot it faster.

Try this once this week: say the slightly brave thing. Ask the question. Send the message. Then notice how little the world reacts.
bank.cta: Tag someone who needs to hear this.

bank.topic: Bernie Madoff: the confession to his sons, the ignored warnings and a 150-year sentence (2008–2009)
bank.hook: December 10, 2008: Bernie Madoff told his sons the business was 'one big lie'. They went to the authorities.
bank.body:
December 10, 2008: Bernie Madoff told his sons the business was "one big lie". They went to the authorities.

The next day he was arrested. Account statements showed almost $65 billion, including fake gains. A whistleblower had warned the SEC for years.

Swipe for the timeline and the one rule that would have protected his investors. Would you have spotted it?
parts: December 10, 2008: Bernie Madoff tells his sons the business is 'one big lie'.
His sons go to the authorities. He's arrested the next day.
He wasn't an outsider. He had once been chairman of Nasdaq. His firm dated back to 1960.
1999: Harry Markopolos tells the SEC Madoff's gains are mathematically impossible.
He keeps warning: 2000, 2001, 2005, 2007. Nothing sticks.
The statements showed almost $65 billion, including fabricated gains. Actual investor losses: about $18 billion by the trustee's estimate.
March 12, 2009: guilty plea to 11 felonies. June 29, 2009: 150 years in prison.
Trustee Irving Picard has recovered and returned more than $14 billion.
The rule: returns that never wobble are a question, not a comfort. Keep your money with an independent custodian you can check.

factCheck: The robbery took place on January 17, 1950, at the Brink's building in Boston's North End.
Eleven people were involved; seven went inside.
Total taken about $2.775 million: about $1.22 million cash, about $1.56 million in checks, money orders and securities.
The robbers entered about 7:10 p.m. and left around 7:30 p.m.
The plan was first conceived in 1947; the group scouted from rooftops and removed locks over months to copy keys.
They made five aborted attempts.
Disguises: chauffeur caps, pea coats, rubber Halloween masks, rubber-soled shoes.
Joseph 'Specs' O'Keefe, shot by a hitman while in hiding, agreed to talk to the FBI on January 6, 1956.
Six suspects were arrested January 12, 1956, five days before the statute of limitations expired.
Eight members received life sentences after an August 1956 trial.
Only about $58,000 was recovered.

factCheck: Dan Ariely described this experiment with students in Predictably Irrational.
The offers were based on The Economist's subscription page: web only $59, print only $125, print + web $125.
With all three options: 16% chose web only, 0% print only, 84% print + web.
Without the print-only option: 68% chose web only and 32% print + web.
The pattern is known as the decoy effect (asymmetric dominance).
The decoy option was never chosen but shifted the other choices.
2026 tie-in is framing, not a statistic.

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. EXT. I-45 — NIGHT (ELEVEN MONTHS LATER)
scenes.text:
Rain. A black Escalade idles under the overpass. Inside, TASHA counts nothing. She just smiles at her phone: a wire confirmation. $20,000,000.00.

MARCUS (V.O.): They say a man can feel it when the ground's about to move. I didn't feel nothing. I was too busy holding the door open for her.

TITLE CARD: THE SETTLEMENT

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT HOUSE, PEARLAND — MORNING (ELEVEN MONTHS EARLIER)
scenes.text:
Sunlight. Grits on the stove. MARCUS, work boots, Grant Air polo, kisses TASHA on the forehead.

TASHA: Invoices for the Fulton job went out?

MARCUS: You tell me. You the brains, I'm just the back.

TASHA (laughing, fixing his collar): And don't you forget it. I got the bills, baby. Go make us some money.

MARCUS (V.O.): Twelve years. I gave her the passwords, the checkbook, the keys to the trucks, the keys to my mama's house. I gave her the keys to me.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT AIR VAN — MOVING — DAY
scenes.text:
KEV rides shotgun, eating sunflower seeds.

KEV: Bro, why the supplier calling ME talking 'bout your card got declined?

MARCUS: Declined? We got forty-eight thousand in savings.

KEV: Then somebody spending it, 'cause it ain't you. You still wearing them boots from '19.

MARCUS: Tasha got it. It's a mix-up.

KEV (spits a shell out the window): A mix-up. Aight.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT HOUSE — KITCHEN — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Marcus slides a bank statement across the island. Small withdrawals circled in red. Three hundred. Eight hundred. Five fifty.

MARCUS: What's all this?

Tasha doesn't blink. She pours him a glass of wine.

TASHA: That's your truck note, your daddy's headstone, and the AC unit you gave Sister Hattie for free. Remember? You told me to handle it.

MARCUS: I... don't remember saying that.

TASHA (soft, rubbing his back): You working sixty hours a week, Marcus. You not remembering right. That's why I got you.

MARCUS (V.O.): And I believed her. 'Cause the alternative was believing my wife was a stranger.

scenes.heading: INT. BEDROOM — 2:07 A.M.
scenes.text: Marcus wakes. Her side of the bed is cold. A sliver of blue light under the door.

scenes.heading: INT. KITCHEN — CONTINUOUS
scenes.text:
He stops in the hallway. Tasha, back turned, whispering into a cheap flip phone he's never seen.

TASHA (low): No, he don't suspect a thing... Just a little longer, Dre. Then it's ours.

She snaps the phone shut. Marcus steps back into the dark before she turns.

MARCUS (V.O.): Dre. Her cousin Dre. The one who only ever came around when he needed something.

scenes.heading: INT. BEDROOM — MOMENTS LATER
scenes.text:
Marcus lies still, eyes open. Tasha slides into bed and drapes her arm across his chest.

TASHA (whispering): Love you, baby.

MARCUS (barely): Love you too.

MARCUS (V.O.): That was the night I should've changed the locks. Instead, I went back to sleep next to the person holding all the keys.

SMASH TO BLACK.

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. INT. GRANT AIR OFFICE — DAY
scenes.text:
Marcus tears the office apart. Drawers on the floor. Kev in the doorway.

MARCUS: The keys to the Fulton job, Kev. I put 'em RIGHT here.

KEV: Bro... that's the third time this week.

MARCUS (V.O.): You don't lose your mind all at once. You lose it in pieces. Somebody just has to keep picking 'em up and hiding 'em.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT HOUSE — LIVING ROOM — NIGHT (ONE WEEK EARLIER)
scenes.text:
Tasha on the couch, laptop open. Marcus walks in, tie loose.

MARCUS: Why you ain't at Mama Pearl's birthday dinner?

TASHA (confused, gentle): Baby... that's next Saturday. You wrote it on the calendar yourself.

She turns the laptop. The family calendar. Next Saturday. In his own shorthand.

MARCUS: I ain't write that.

TASHA: Marcus. Look at me. Are you sleeping?

scenes.heading: INT. MAMA PEARL'S HOUSE — THIRD WARD — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Candles burned down on a cake nobody cut. MAMA PEARL sits alone at a set table.

MAMA PEARL (on the phone): My son ain't never missed my birthday in thirty-eight years. Not once.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT HOUSE — BATHROOM — SAME TIME
scenes.text:
Tasha in the mirror, phone to her ear. Calm as Sunday.

TASHA: He's tired, Mama Pearl. He's been forgetting a lot. I'm worried, honestly.

She hangs up. Then texts: "Seed planted." The reply pops up: DRE: "thats my girl. need 600 tho."

scenes.heading: INT. BARBERSHOP — SATURDAY
scenes.text:
Clippers buzzing. Kev in the next chair.

KEV: Man, your wife told my wife you might need to "talk to somebody." Like a doctor.

MARCUS: She said that?

BARBER (not looking up): She said it to half the shop, big dog.

MARCUS (V.O.): She wasn't hiding it. She was announcing it. Building the story before I even knew there was one.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT HOUSE — KITCHEN — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Marcus opens the junk drawer for a lighter. Freezes. The Fulton keys. Sitting right on top.

MARCUS: Tasha. Come here.

She walks in, sees the keys, and puts a hand over her heart.

TASHA: Oh, thank God. See? You put 'em in here and forgot. Baby, I'm making you an appointment Monday. No arguments.

MARCUS: I ain't been in that drawer in a month.

TASHA (tears up on cue): Do you hear yourself? I'm trying to help you and you looking at me like I'm the enemy.

Marcus folds. Pulls her in.

MARCUS: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, baby.

Over his shoulder, Tasha's face goes flat. Empty. She checks the time on the microwave.

MARCUS (V.O.): I apologized. To the woman who put the keys there. That's how good she was.

scenes.heading: EXT. GRANT HOUSE — DRIVEWAY — LATER
scenes.text:
Kev's truck idles at the curb. He watches a silver Charger pull up two houses down. A man in fresh Jordans steps out, looks at the Grant house, and makes a call.

KEV (to himself): Now who in the world is you?

SMASH TO BLACK.

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. INT. GRANT HOUSE — MASTER CLOSET — DAY
scenes.text:
Marcus on his knees, flashlight in his teeth, behind a row of Tasha's heels. His hand closes on a shoebox. Inside: a cheap flip phone, charging cable, and a stack of prepaid cards.

MARCUS (V.O.): Twelve years married and I'd never touched her side of the closet. Respect, I called it. Turns out it was just a good hiding place.

scenes.heading: INT. CLOSET — CONTINUOUS
scenes.text:
He opens the phone. One contact. "D." Hundreds of texts.

ON SCREEN (TEXTS): D: "he sign it yet"  TASHA: "not yet. he trusts me tho"  D: "trust is the whole play baby"

The garage door rumbles. Marcus snaps the phone shut, shoves the box back, kills the flashlight.

scenes.heading: INT. KITCHEN — MOMENTS LATER
scenes.text:
Tasha drops grocery bags. Studies him. Something in his face.

TASHA: Why you sweating like that?

MARCUS: AC on the fritz in the bedroom.

TASHA (smiling slowly): The AC man's AC broke. That's funny.

scenes.heading: EXT. BACKYARD — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Marcus and Kev at the grill. Low voices.

KEV: Silver Charger. Jordans. Been parked down the street three times this month.

MARCUS: That's Dre. Her cousin.

KEV: Cousin? Bro, I saw that "cousin" kiss her at the gas station on Almeda. And it wasn't no family reunion kiss.

Marcus grips the tongs so hard his knuckles go pale.

MARCUS (V.O.): The whole time I thought I was going crazy. I wasn't crazy. I was outnumbered.

scenes.heading: INT. MASTER BEDROOM — LATER
scenes.text:
Marcus comes in. Tasha sits on the edge of the bed. The shoebox is open on the comforter. The phone, in her hand.

TASHA (calm): You went in my closet.

MARCUS: Who is D, Tasha?

TASHA: D is my DOCTOR, Marcus. Dr. Daniels. My therapist.

MARCUS: Your therapist asking if I signed something?

TASHA (standing, voice rising): The life insurance! I told you three times we needed to update it after your daddy passed. And you forgot. Again. So yes, I talk to somebody about how scared I am that my husband is losing his mind!

She's crying now. Real tears. Perfect tears.

TASHA: You went through my things like I'm a criminal. Do you know how that feels?

Marcus stares at her. For the first time, he doesn't fold.

MARCUS: Then call Dr. Daniels. Right now. Speaker.

Silence. The longest three seconds of their marriage.

Tasha wipes her eyes. Hands him the phone.

TASHA: Go ahead.

Marcus presses call. It rings. Once. Twice. A WOMAN answers, professional and warm.

WOMAN (V.O., PHONE): Dr. Daniels' office, after-hours line.

Marcus's face falls. Tasha folds her arms.

MARCUS (V.O.): She was ready. She'd been ready for months. And I'd just walked right into the trap she built for me.

SMASH TO BLACK.

scenes.text:
A tow truck backs up to Marcus's work van. Marcus runs out in his undershirt.

MARCUS: Ay! AY! That's my van, man!

MARCUS (V.O.): I'd paid that van off in 2022. I had the title in a frame on my office wall. Or I used to.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT AIR OFFICE — CONTINUOUS
scenes.text: Marcus stares at the wall. An empty nail where the framed title hung.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT HOUSE — KITCHEN — MORNING
scenes.text:
The house phone rings. Then his cell. Then the house phone again. Marcus answers.

COLLECTOR (V.O., PHONE): Marcus Grant? Calling about your Capital Rewards card. Balance of thirty-one thousand, four hundred...

MARCUS: I don't HAVE a Capital Rewards card.

COLLECTOR (V.O., PHONE): Opened in March, sir. Your social, your signature, your address.

Tasha walks in, robe on, sips coffee.

TASHA: Who is it, baby?

Marcus covers the phone.

MARCUS: Thirty-one thousand on a card I never opened.

TASHA (eyes wide, horrified): Oh my God. Somebody stole your identity? Marcus, I told you to stop giving your card to every supply house in Houston.

MARCUS (V.O.): She didn't even flinch. Just picked up the story and finished it for me.

scenes.heading: INT. MAMA PEARL'S HOUSE — DAY
scenes.text:
Marcus at her kitchen table, papers everywhere. Mama Pearl reads one slowly, glasses on her nose.

MAMA PEARL: Baby. This one's a loan. Against my house.

MARCUS: That's not possible, Mama.

MAMA PEARL: It's got my name. And yours, as co-signer. And this signature right here...

She slides it across. Her handwriting. Almost.

MAMA PEARL: I ain't signed nothing since your daddy's funeral. And who was sitting right here, helping me with all them papers that week?

Marcus closes his eyes.

MARCUS: Tasha.

MAMA PEARL: I'ma say this one time, 'cause I'm saved. That girl smile with her teeth, never her eyes.

scenes.heading: EXT. GALLERIA PARKING GARAGE — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Dre leans on the silver Charger. Tasha walks up, hands him an envelope. Thick.

DRE: This it?

TASHA: That's the van money. Mama Pearl's loan clears Friday.

DRE (counting): You know he gon' figure it out.

TASHA: He figures out a piece at a time. And every piece I make him look a little crazier. By the time he figures out the whole thing, nobody'll believe a word he says.

Dre pulls her close.

DRE: That's why I love you.

TASHA (pulling away, cold): You love what I bring you. Don't get it twisted.

Across the garage, a phone camera lens catches the light behind a pillar. KEV, recording.

MARCUS (V.O.): She was right about one thing. Nobody believed a man who sounded crazy. But they might believe a video.

SMASH TO BLACK.

She sat her "cousin" at the head of his Sunday table. Then the baby monitor caught the plan: accidents happen every day on I-45.

Episode 6 is next. Follow so you don't miss it. 👀

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. INT. GRANT HOUSE — SUNDAY DINNER — DAY
scenes.text:
The table set like a magazine. Tasha's famous oxtails. At the end of the table, in Marcus's chair: DRE, fresh fade, gold chain, laughing too loud.

DRE: Cuz! Pass them greens, big man.

Marcus doesn't move.

MARCUS (V.O.): She invited him. To my table. On a Sunday. Like a dare.

scenes.heading: INT. DINING ROOM — CONTINUOUS
scenes.text:
TASHA: Dre's staying with us a couple weeks. He lost his apartment. Family helps family, right baby?

MARCUS: Family.

DRE (grinning): I won't be no trouble. I'll even help out at the shop. I'm good with my hands.

Kev, across the table, nearly chokes on his tea.

KEV: Good with your hands, huh? Doing what?

DRE (cold, still smiling): Whatever needs doing, OG.

scenes.heading: INT. GARAGE — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Marcus and Kev, door down, one bulb.

Kev holds up his phone: the Galleria garage video. The envelope. The kiss. Tasha's voice, clear: "...nobody'll believe a word he says."

KEV: That's it, bro. That's the whole case. Take this to a lawyer tomorrow.

MARCUS: And say what? My wife been playing me for three years and I ain't noticed 'til my boy filmed it?

KEV: Say it however you want. Just SAY it.

Marcus takes the phone. Watches it again. His jaw works.

MARCUS: Not yet.

KEV: Not YET?

MARCUS: I go to a lawyer now, she gets half of nothing and walks. I want to know what she's really after. The van, the cards, Mama's house... that's change. Somebody this patient is waiting on something big.

MARCUS (V.O.): For three years she'd been playing chess. For the first time, I moved a piece.

scenes.heading: INT. GUEST ROOM — LATE NIGHT
scenes.text:
Dre on the bed, counting cash. Tasha slips in, closes the door.

DRE: This little drip ain't enough, Tash. Van money. Card money. I got people I owe.

TASHA: I told you. Patience. The life insurance paperwork is almost done.

DRE: Insurance pay when somebody DIE.

Beat. Tasha says nothing.

DRE (leaning in): Or when somebody get HURT. Real bad. Accidents happen every day on I-45.

TASHA (sharp): I didn't sign up for that.

DRE: You signed up for twenty years of being broke? 'Cause that's the other option.

Tasha stares at him a long time. Then, quietly:

TASHA: Nobody gets killed.

DRE (smiling): Nobody gets killed.

scenes.heading: INT. HALLWAY — CONTINUOUS
scenes.text: The hallway is dark. Empty. But the baby monitor Marcus never took down from the nursery glows green on the shelf. Its partner sits on Marcus's nightstand, volume up.

scenes.heading: INT. MASTER BEDROOM — CONTINUOUS
scenes.text:
Marcus sits on the edge of the bed in the dark, the monitor's speaker crackling in his hand.

MARCUS (V.O.): Accidents happen every day on I-45. I just didn't know which one of us they had in mind.

SMASH TO BLACK.

series.title: Red Light
series.logline: They planned an accident for him. One rainy night on Telephone Road, a different one found her.
series.nextTime: Tasha wakes up. And a lawyer in a $4,000 suit is already at her bedside.
series.caption:

They planned an accident for him. One rainy night on Telephone Road, a different one found her.

Episode 7 is next. Follow so you don't miss it. 👀

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. EXT. TELEPHONE RD & I-45 — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Rain like the sky is mad at somebody. A traffic light turns red. A white sedan rolls into the intersection. Headlights fill the frame from the left. Air horn. Brakes screaming.

IMPACT.

Glass in slow motion.

MARCUS (V.O.): They planned an accident for me. God had a different one in mind.

TITLE CARD: SIX HOURS EARLIER

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT AIR OFFICE — AFTERNOON
scenes.text:
Tasha leans in the doorway, sweet as pie.

TASHA: Baby, the warehouse on Telephone Road called. Their whole system's down. They'll pay double if you come tonight. Around ten?

MARCUS: Ten. In the rain.

TASHA: Take the van. I'll keep your plate warm.

She kisses him. Walks out. Marcus stares at the door.

MARCUS (V.O.): There ain't no warehouse calling a one-man shop at ten o'clock at night in a storm. Not unless somebody wants that one man on the highway.

scenes.heading: INT. KEV'S TRUCK — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Marcus and Kev parked in a dark lot facing the Telephone Road exit. Wipers on low.

KEV: So we just sit here?

MARCUS: We sit. We watch. Whoever's waiting on me is gon' get tired of waiting.

Across the road, under the overpass: the silver Charger. Lights off. Dre behind the wheel, checking his phone.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT HOUSE — SAME TIME
scenes.text:
Tasha paces. Calls Marcus. Voicemail. Calls again. Voicemail. She calls Dre.

TASHA: Is he there?

DRE (V.O., PHONE): Van ain't showed. Something wrong, Tash.

TASHA: He never misses a paid job. Never.

DRE (V.O., PHONE): Unless he know.

The word lands. Tasha grabs her keys.

TASHA: Don't move. I'm coming.

scenes.heading: EXT. TELEPHONE RD — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Kev points. A white sedan, Tasha's car, speeding toward the overpass.

KEV: That's your wife, bro.

Marcus sits up. The light ahead turns yellow. Tasha's on the phone, not looking. Yellow. Red. She doesn't stop.

From the left, an eighteen-wheeler, LONE STAR FREIGHT on the trailer, comes off the ramp too fast. Its light is red too. The driver's face glows blue from a phone in his hand.

MARCUS: No. NO!

IMPACT.

The sedan spins, crumples against the guardrail. Silence except for rain and a horn stuck on.

Under the overpass, the silver Charger's headlights snap on. Dre peels out the other way. Gone.

scenes.heading: EXT. CRASH SITE — MOMENTS LATER
scenes.text:
Marcus runs through the rain, slides on his knees at the driver's door. Tasha, bloody, eyes fluttering.

MARCUS: Tasha. Tasha, look at me. I'm right here. I'm right here, baby.

TASHA (barely a whisper): You... weren't... supposed to be...

Her eyes close. Sirens rise. Red and blue wash over Marcus's face.

MARCUS (V.O.): She spent three years trying to break me. And there I was, on my knees in the rain, praying she'd live. That's the part nobody tells you about love. It don't leave just 'cause it should.

SMASH TO BLACK.

Twenty million dollars from the trucking company. She almost died for it, and the first thing she did was plan how to keep it from him.

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. INT. LAW OFFICES OF WHITFIELD & PRYOR — DOWNTOWN HOUSTON — DAY (FOUR MONTHS LATER)
scenes.text:
A glass conference room forty floors up. Tasha, cane beside her chair, a healing scar along her jaw. RENEE WHITFIELD slides a single sheet across the table.

RENEE: Lone Star Freight settled. Their driver was nineteen hours into a fourteen-hour shift, phone in his hand, running a red. They didn't want a jury to see that video.

Tasha reads the number. Her hand trembles.

RENEE: Twenty million dollars, Mrs. Grant.

MARCUS (V.O.): She almost died for that money. And the first thing she did when she got it... was plan how to keep it from me.

scenes.heading: INT. MEMORIAL HERMANN HOSPITAL — ROOM 614 — FOUR MONTHS EARLIER
scenes.text:
Tasha wakes to beeping machines. Marcus asleep in the chair, still in the clothes from the crash. Flowers from the church. A card from Mama Pearl: "Praying for you."

Tasha looks at him. Something cracks in her face. Just for a second. Then a knock.

Renee Whitfield, $4,000 suit, business card already out.

RENEE: Mrs. Grant. I'm sorry to come so soon. But the trucking company's insurers were here before your surgery was over. You need someone on your side.

scenes.heading: INT. HOSPITAL ROOM — LATER
scenes.text:
Marcus brings back two coffees. Renee's gone. Tasha's sitting up.

TASHA: I hired a lawyer.

MARCUS: Good. They need to pay for what they did to you.

TASHA (carefully): The case is in my name only. Renee says it's cleaner.

MARCUS: Whatever helps you heal.

MARCUS (V.O.): I meant it. That's the crazy part. I still meant it.

scenes.heading: INT. HOSPITAL PARKING GARAGE — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Dre waits by the elevator, hood up. Tasha comes down in a wheelchair, a nurse pushing. She waves the nurse off.

DRE: You good? I been worried sick.

TASHA (cold): You drove away. I was bleeding in that car and you drove AWAY.

DRE: I couldn't be there when the cops came, you know that! Tash, this the come-up. Twenty million, maybe more. We was gon' do it the hard way and God handed it to us.

TASHA: "We."

DRE: We, baby. Like always.

Tasha stares at him. Then smiles. The old smile. The one that never reaches her eyes.

TASHA: Like always.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT HOUSE — OFFICE — NIGHT (PRESENT DAY)
scenes.text:
Marcus at his desk, a box of old Grant Air invoices. He pulls out a folder. The life insurance application Tasha pushed him to sign. He never did. Clipped to it, a second policy. On Tasha. Beneficiary: Andre Lockett.

MARCUS (quietly): She ain't the only one with a plan.

His phone buzzes. A text from an unknown number.

ON SCREEN: "Your wife got 20M. You want to know what really happened that night? Meet me. Come alone."

SMASH TO BLACK.

series.logline: Divorce papers, every stolen debt in his name, and a tow-truck driver with dashcam footage somebody paid $5,000 to bury.

series.caption:

Divorce papers, every stolen debt in his name, and a tow-truck driver with dashcam footage somebody paid $5,000 to bury.

Episode 9 is next. Follow so you don't miss it. 👀

Whose side are you on? 👇

(A fictional story. Any resemblance to real people is coincidental. Voices are AI.)

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. INT. GRANT AIR OFFICE — DAY
scenes.text:
A PROCESS SERVER in a Rockets cap drops an envelope on Marcus's desk.

PROCESS SERVER: Marcus Grant? You've been served.

Marcus opens it. PETITION FOR DIVORCE. Tasha Renee Grant v. Marcus Anthony Grant. Attached: a list of debts. The van. The Capital Rewards card. Mama Pearl's loan. Every one of them filed under "Respondent's separate obligations."

MARCUS (V.O.): She kept the twenty million. And left me every dollar she ever stole.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT HOUSE — DAY
scenes.text:
Half-empty rooms. Tasha's closet bare. On the kitchen island, her wedding ring and a note in her perfect handwriting: "I deserve to be happy. Don't contact me except through Renee."

Kev reads it over Marcus's shoulder.

KEV: "I deserve to be happy." With YOUR money? With Mama Pearl's HOUSE?

MARCUS: With her money now. The settlement's in her name. Separate property. Renee made sure.

KEV: Then show 'em the video. The garage. The envelope. ALL of it.

MARCUS: The video shows a woman handing her cousin cash. Her lawyer will eat that alive. I need the night of the crash.

scenes.heading: EXT. FIFTH WARD — TOW YARD — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Chain-link fence. Rows of wrecks. Marcus alone, as the text told him. A man steps out of the office: JEROME, 50s, grease-stained jumpsuit, toothpick.

JEROME: You the husband.

MARCUS: You the one texting me.

JEROME: I'm the one who got to that wreck first. Rotation tow. Been doing it twenty-two years. My truck got a dashcam front and back.

MARCUS: And you sat on it four months?

JEROME: I sat on it 'cause a man in a silver Charger came by my yard the next morning and offered me five thousand dollars to lose it.

Marcus goes still.

JEROME: I took his money. I ain't gon' lie to you. But I didn't lose nothing. Then I saw your wife on the news, crying about the truck company. And I saw you on your knees in the rain on my footage. Man... I got daughters. I couldn't let it ride.

He holds out a flash drive.

MARCUS: What's on it?

JEROME: Everything before the crash. The Charger waiting under the bridge. That boy on the phone. And your wife, on HER phone, running that red too.

MARCUS (V.O.): The truck company paid twenty million because they thought it was all their fault. It wasn't all their fault.

scenes.heading: INT. MARCUS'S TRUCK — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Marcus holds the flash drive under the dome light. His phone rings. TASHA.

He answers. Silence. Then:

TASHA (V.O., PHONE): You went to see the tow man.

Marcus's eyes snap to the mirror. Headlights behind him. Close.

TASHA (V.O., PHONE): Give me that drive, Marcus. And I'll make all your debts disappear. Mama Pearl keeps her house. Everybody wins.

MARCUS: Everybody but the truth.

TASHA (V.O., PHONE) (soft, almost sad): The truth ain't never paid nobody's bills, baby.

The headlights behind him flip to high beams. A silver Charger.

SMASH TO BLACK.

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. EXT. LOOP 610 — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Marcus's truck weaves through traffic. The silver Charger glued to his bumper, high beams blazing. Dre leans on the horn.

MARCUS (V.O.): They say never run from a man who has nothing to lose. Dre had everything to lose. That's worse.

Marcus jerks the wheel. Cuts across three lanes onto the Gessner exit. The Charger overshoots, brakes, horns blaring behind it.

scenes.heading: EXT. HOUSTON POLICE DEPARTMENT — MIDWEST STATION — CONTINUOUS
scenes.text: Marcus pulls into the lit lot and parks right under the camera pole. He sits there, breathing hard. The Charger slows at the curb. Idles. Then pulls away.

scenes.heading: INT. KEV'S APARTMENT — LATE NIGHT
scenes.text:
Kev, Marcus and Mama Pearl crowded around a laptop. The flash drive plugged in. Jerome's dashcam, timestamped.

ON SCREEN (DASHCAM): 10:41 P.M. The silver Charger parked under the overpass, lights off.  10:52 P.M. Dre on the phone, animated.  10:56 P.M. Tasha's white sedan approaching, phone to her ear. The light turns red. She doesn't slow down.  10:56:14 P.M. The truck. The impact.  10:56:20 P.M. The Charger's lights snap on. It leaves.

Mama Pearl puts her hand over her mouth.

MAMA PEARL: Lord, have mercy. She ran it too.

KEV: The truck ran a red. She ran a red. And her "cousin" was sitting under the bridge waiting on YOU.

MARCUS: And a man offered Jerome five thousand dollars to make this disappear. That's not grief. That's a cover-up.

KEV: So what now? Cops?

Marcus shakes his head slowly.

MARCUS: The trucking company. Their lawyers paid twenty million thinking the whole crash was their fault. If they see this...

MAMA PEARL (quietly): They'll take it all back.

MARCUS (V.O.): I could burn her whole world down with one email. And for the first time in a year, I had to ask myself what kind of man I wanted to be.

scenes.heading: INT. TASHA'S NEW PENTHOUSE — GALLERIA — SAME NIGHT
scenes.text:
Floor-to-ceiling glass. Tasha on a white couch, wine untouched. Dre storms in, sweating.

DRE: He got away. He went to the police station, Tash! He sitting on that tape!

TASHA (icy): You chased him? On the freeway? After I told you to let me handle it?

DRE: You ain't handling NOTHING! You sitting up here in a penthouse while my name all over that video!

Tasha stands. Walks to the window. Her reflection over the city lights.

TASHA: Your name. Not mine. You were the one waiting under the bridge. You were the one offering bribes. All I did was run a light.

Dre's face changes. He finally sees her.

DRE: You setting me up.

TASHA (turning, smiling): Baby. I been setting everybody up.

Dre reaches into his jacket. Tasha doesn't flinch. Behind her, on the kitchen counter, her phone screen glows. Recording.

SMASH TO BLACK.

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. INT. TASHA'S PENTHOUSE — CONTINUOUS
scenes.text:
Dre's hand comes out of his jacket. Not a gun. His phone. Screen lit. Recording.

DRE: You thought you was the only one taping? I got every voice note, Tash. "Seed planted." "Nobody gets killed." Every one.

For the first time all season, Tasha has no line ready.

MARCUS (V.O.): Two people who built their whole lives on lies, standing in a glass box, holding the truth like a weapon. Neither one of 'em knew I was already holding the biggest one.

scenes.heading: INT. WHITFIELD & PRYOR — CONFERENCE ROOM — NEXT MORNING
scenes.text:
Renee Whitfield at the head of the table. Across from her: two LONE STAR FREIGHT ATTORNEYS and an ASSISTANT DISTRICT ATTORNEY. A laptop plays Jerome's dashcam. Tasha's car. The red light. The Charger leaving.

LONE STAR ATTORNEY: Your client ran the same red light. And her associate was positioned to cause a collision with her husband. We settled based on a lie of omission, Counselor.

Renee closes her folder. Calmly.

RENEE: I'll need to speak with my client.

scenes.heading: INT. HALLWAY — CONTINUOUS
scenes.text:
Renee, low, to Tasha:

RENEE: You never told me about the cousin. Or the bridge. The settlement's getting reopened, and the DA wants to talk about conspiracy. Your best move is to cooperate.

TASHA: Cooperate how?

RENEE: Tell them everything about Andre Lockett. Before he tells them everything about you.

Tasha looks through the glass. Across the lobby, Dre sits with a public defender, staring right at her.

scenes.heading: INT. MAMA PEARL'S PORCH — THIRD WARD — THREE MONTHS LATER
scenes.text:
Sunday afternoon. Mama Pearl rocks, Bible in her lap. Marcus climbs the steps with a folder.

MARCUS: The bank voided the loan, Mama. Forged signature. The house is yours. Free and clear.

Mama Pearl closes her eyes.

MAMA PEARL: Thank you, Jesus. And thank you, baby.

MARCUS (V.O.): Lone Star clawed back the settlement. Dre took a plea: attempted bribery and insurance fraud conspiracy, seven years. Tasha testified against him and walked out with probation, her medical bills paid, and nothing else. Twenty million dollars, gone like it was never real. Because it never was.

scenes.heading: EXT. GRANT AIR — NEW SHOP — DAY
scenes.text:
A new sign goes up: GRANT AIR & HEATING. Kev on the ladder, Marcus steadying it. Two new vans in the lot.

KEV: You ever think about her?

MARCUS: Every time I lock up.

A white sedan pulls up to the curb. The window rolls down. Tasha, scar faded, sunglasses on.

TASHA: You still got a key to the old house?

MARCUS: Changed the locks.

She almost smiles. A real one, this time. It reaches her eyes, then dies there.

TASHA: Good. You learned something.

She drives off.

MARCUS (V.O.): She was right. I did learn something. Love will give anybody the keys. Wisdom checks who's holding 'em.

FADE OUT.

scenes.heading: POST-CREDITS. INT. TASHA'S CAR — MOMENTS LATER
scenes.text:
Tasha's phone buzzes. Unknown number.

ON SCREEN: "The Lone Star driver wasn't on his phone by accident. Somebody paid him to be on that road. Want to know who? Season 2."

Tasha slowly takes off her sunglasses.

SMASH TO BLACK.

scenes.heading: COLD OPEN. INT. GRANT AIR & HEATING — NIGHT · NOW
scenes.text:
Marcus locks up the new shop. On the corkboard, one faded photo he never took down: a girl in a yellow sundress, holding a broken box fan.

MARCUS (V.O.): Everybody asks how I didn't see it coming. Truth is, I saw her. August, 2013. I just didn't know what I was looking at.

scenes.heading: THIRTEEN YEARS EARLIER. EXT. MIDTOWN APARTMENTS — AUGUST 2013 · DAY
scenes.text:
A hundred and three degrees. Unit 3B. The door's already open. Tasha sits on the floor by a dead box fan, a notebook in her lap.

TASHA: You the AC man? You forty minutes late. I wrote it down.

MARCUS: Traffic on 59, ma'am.

TASHA (not looking up): Don't call me ma'am. I'm twenty-five, not your auntie.

scenes.heading: INT. UNIT 3B — LATER
scenes.text:
MARCUS: Twelve-dollar part. My company charges a hundred and eighty-nine.

Her notebook: every bill, every due date, to the penny. She counts out the cash. Twice.

TASHA (quiet): My mama moved us eleven times before I was fifteen. I'm never being broke again. Not for nobody.

By the door, a pair of men's Jordans. Size twelve.

TASHA: My cousin's. He stays here sometimes.

MARCUS (V.O.): Cousin. First time I heard that word out of her mouth. I didn't think about it again for twelve years.

scenes.heading: INT. MAMA PEARL'S CHURCH — THIRD WARD · SUNDAY
scenes.text:
Sunday. Tasha, in yellow, walks straight down the aisle holding his screwdriver.

TASHA (whispering): You left this. Figured a man who don't charge for his time might need his tools.

MAMA PEARL (low): Who is THAT?

MAMA PEARL: Pretty girl. Smart girl. She counted the room before she counted the hymns.

scenes.heading: EXT. EMANCIPATION PARK — NIGHT
scenes.text:
Fried catfish on the hood of his old Silverado. String lights in the oaks.

MARCUS: One day it's gon' be my name on the van. Grant Air. My own trucks. My own crew.

TASHA (leaning in): You got the hands. I got the head. Baby, together we'd be dangerous.

MARCUS (V.O.): She was the first person who ever said my dream out loud like it was already real.

scenes.heading: INT. KEV'S CAR — NIGHT
scenes.text:
KEV: Second time I ever met her, she asked me how much you clear a week.

MARCUS: She's good with money, Kev. That's a good thing.

KEV: Being good with money and being good with YOUR money is two different things.

scenes.heading: INT. MARCUS'S FIRST APARTMENT — CHRISTMAS EVE 2013
scenes.text:
No ring. He can't afford one. Just a small box. Inside: one brass key on a red ribbon.

MARCUS: It ain't a diamond. It's my front door. I want you to have the key.

TASHA (barely): Nobody ever gave me nothing I didn't have to take.

MARCUS (V.O.): I've played those tears back a thousand times. I still think they were real.

scenes.heading: INT. THE WEDDING — JUNE 2014
scenes.text:
The bride's side, nearly empty. And in the last row, a young man in fresh Jordans who never stands, never claps, never signs the guest book.

MARCUS (V.O.): Her cousin, Dre. One more person I'd get to know a whole lot better.

scenes.heading: INT. GRANT AIR & HEATING — NIGHT · NOW
scenes.text:
Now. Kev plays the old wedding video and freezes on the back row.

KEV: Marcus. Look at who Dre is talking to.

Next to Dre: a skinny nineteen-year-old in a Lone Star Freight cap.

MARCUS (slowly): That's the driver.

KEV: At YOUR wedding.

MARCUS (V.O.): Maybe she loved me. But somebody had a plan the day I said I do.

SMASH TO BLACK.
